I'm planning implementation of Story 8.3 "Profile Name Editing" for a Flutter app called Cerne (reflective journaling app, Clean Architecture, flutter_bloc, fpdart Either, repositories, hive_ce for cache in other features but NOT dashboard/account). I need a distilled investigation report (not a full file dump) covering exactly these things, each with concrete file paths and line numbers/symbol names:

1. **Current account settings screen state**: Read `lib/features/account/presentation/screens/account_settings_screen.dart` fully. Describe its current structure — widgets, state management, how the user's display name is currently shown (if at all), existing constructor params, cubits it uses, the avatar widget usage (52px per epic context — find where it's currently used/built), and the `_announce` helper mentioned in other specs.

2. **Account feature layer structure**: List all files under `lib/features/account/` (domain/data/presentation). Is there already a repository/use case for reading or updating profile/display name? If a `User`/`Profile` entity already exists elsewhere (e.g. auth feature), where, and what fields does it have?

3. **Backend contract for name editing**: Read `docs/input/backend/api/openapi.yaml` and find the operation(s) related to updating the user's profile/display name (look for PATCH/PUT on something like `/account` or `/profile` or `/user`). Report: the operation id, path, `x-cerne-function` value, request body schema (fields), response schema, security requirement (bearerAuth?), and any error codes documented. Also check `docs/input/backend/README.md` for the path-to-function mapping entry for this operation.

4. **Requirements doc**: Search `docs/input/requirements.md` for the FR covering profile name editing (likely near FR for account/dashboard, search for "name", "perfil", "profile", "editing"). Quote the exact FR text and acceptance criteria verbatim, and note its FR number.

5. **Prototype UX reference**: Search `docs/input/prototype/prototype-extract.md` and if needed the raw `docs/input/prototype/cerne-prototype.html` for the inline name-editing interaction — pencil icon toggling to a check icon, inline text field behavior, confirm/tap-away-to-revert behavior. Quote relevant markup/CSS classes, exact token names/values (font, size, color) used for this specific UI piece, and any JS behavior describing the edit/confirm/cancel flow (e.g. function names like `editName`/`saveName` if present). Also check if there's a dedicated input-field design token already in `lib/core/design_tokens.dart` I should reuse (search that file for anything related to text fields/inputs already defined, e.g. used by chat composer or other inline edit affordances).

6. **Existing similar patterns to reuse**: Is there any existing inline-editable text field pattern anywhere else in `lib/` (grep for TextEditingController usage, inline edit patterns)? Is there a shared `Resource<T>` pattern used elsewhere for a single async action (not just fetch) — e.g. submitting a value and getting back success/failure — look at how chat message retry or bookmark-to-entry (spec-6-4) or export request (spec-7-1) handle a "fire an action, get Either<Failure, T> back, show loading/error" cubit shape, since this story likely needs something similar (fire PATCH, show saving state, handle success/failure) rather than a pure fetch-on-load cubit like DashboardCubit/DashboardNarrativeCubit.

7. **Existing account_settings_screen_test.dart**: skim `test/features/account/presentation/screens/account_settings_screen_test.dart` structure (fake repository pattern, how cubits are constructed in tests) so a planner knows how new tests would slot in.

8. **account_injection.dart or equivalent DI file**: find and report the DI registration file for the account feature (search for `account_injection.dart` or similar), and how `AccountSettingsScreen` is routed in `lib/core/navigation/app_router.dart`.

Report back concisely with file:line references for everything found. Do not write any files — this is pure investigation. Keep your final report under 500 lines, organized by the numbered sections above.

## Conventions that differ from defaults

- Call the backend only at `{FUNCTIONS_BASE_URL}/<x-cerne-function>`, never at the literal REST path shown in `openapi.yaml` — each operation's real URL is its `x-cerne-function` name, with path parameters appended as trailing segments. Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When not to use

If the target is already known, use the direct tool: Read for a known path, `grep` via the Bash tool for a specific symbol or string. Reserve this tool for open-ended questions that span the codebase, or tasks that match an available agent type.

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- Agents run in the background by default. When an agent runs in the background, you will be automatically notified when it completes — do NOT sleep, poll, or proactively check on its progress. Continue with other work or respond to the user instead.
- **Foreground vs background**: Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — e.g., a research agent whose finding gates the edit you're about to make. Otherwise let it run in the background (the default) — this includes fire-and-forget work, independent investigations, and anything where the user might hand you something else in the meantime. Wanting the result "next" is not enough on its own.
- **Don't race**: after launching a background agent, you know nothing about its results. Never fabricate or predict them in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The completion notification arrives in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks before it lands, say the agent is still running — give status, not a guess.

- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option).
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent

</commentary>

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. # Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TodoWrite or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so

- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TodoWrite or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

EOF
)"

Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. # Epic 8 Context: Evolution Dashboard & Account Management

<!-- Compiled from planning artifacts. Edit freely. Regenerate with compile-epic-context if planning docs change. -->

## Goal

Users can see an on-demand chart of their journaling activity with an independent AI narrative, edit their display name, log out, and permanently delete their account and all associated data. This is the final build unit in the delivery order — it assumes every earlier unit (entries, auth, chat, export) already exists, since the dashboard has nothing to aggregate without entries and account actions rely on the auth session already established in F000.

## Stories

- Story 8.1: On-Demand Dashboard Aggregation Across Entry Counts
- Story 8.2: Independent Narrative Text & Narrative-Unavailable State
- Story 8.3: Profile Name Editing
- Story 8.4: Logout
- Story 8.5: Account Deletion

## Requirements & Constraints

- The evolution chart is computed fresh every time the settings screen opens — never served from a stale local cache — and must render correctly at exactly three entry-count scenarios: zero, one, and more than thirty. These counts are fixed and not re-tunable.
- The narrative paragraph is a separate network call from the chart data, by design: the two must never be coupled so that a narrative failure cannot block or hide a chart that has valid data.
- Aggregation must recalculate whenever a new entry is created anywhere in the app; because entries are immutable (never edited), invalidation only ever needs to trigger on create.
- Account deletion is a hard, permanent delete of the account and all associated data (LGPD-driven) — not a soft delete or deactivation.
- No dedicated "account deleted" confirmation screen exists for this delivery; both logout and account deletion dead-end at the same login/vault destination.
- The persona selector shown on this screen is a cosmetic, non-functional placeholder only (an extension feature) — it must never appear to change assistant behavior.
- Every acceptance criterion for this epic's FRs must pass as the primary success measure; no automated performance instrumentation is required beyond a manual spot-check against the product's general UI-latency thresholds.
- Standard cross-cutting rules apply: no Clean Architecture layer violations, repository methods return `Either<Failure, T>` with no unmapped exceptions, and no visual value is hardcoded outside the design-tokens source.

## Technical Decisions

- Two features own this epic's work: a `dashboard` feature (chart + narrative aggregation/rendering) and a separate `account` feature (persona-toggle placeholder, profile edit, logout, delete account). Both are thin — standard layer-dependency and Either-error-channel rules apply, nothing feature-specific beyond that.
- The dashboard screen uses the shared `Resource<T>` (`idle`/`loading`/`data`/`error`) view-state type, since it is a single-source, single-fetch-lifecycle screen — do not build a one-off state shape for it, and do not force the narrative fetch into the same `Resource<T>` instance as the chart (they are independent fetches, each can be its own `Resource<T>` if a second one is needed).
- The dashboard is explicitly excluded from the local offline-cache pattern used by entries/chat — it has no `hive_ce` box and is never served from cache; each screen visit is a live fetch. Cache-invalidation behavior for the chart (recalculating after a new entry) is a presentation-layer concern owned by whoever builds this epic, not a shared local-cache mechanism.
- This epic extends the minimal settings-screen stub already scaffolded earlier in the project rather than recreating the screen.
- The 52px avatar shown here reuses the same avatar component already built earlier (previously only used at a 40px size) — do not reimplement it.
- Charting uses `fl_chart` (already pinned for the project).

## UX & Interaction Patterns

- Dashboard empty/sparse states: zero entries shows a placeholder chart icon and "Comece a registrar..." with no summary text at all (nothing to summarize, not a failure); exactly one entry shows a single bar with "Ainda é cedo pra ver um padrão..."; more than thirty entries shows a 10-bar chart with the AI narrative paragraph below it.
- Narrative-unavailable is a distinct visual state from the zero-entries empty state: when only the narrative call fails, the chart still renders normally and a clear "narrative unavailable" message appears in its place — never a blank space, never conflated with having no data.
- Profile name editing: tapping the pencil icon beside the name switches it to an inline editable field and the pencil icon itself changes to a check icon — the only place in the product where an icon's meaning changes rather than just its color. Confirming saves and reverts to display mode; tapping away without confirming also reverts to display mode. There is no separate "edit profile" screen.
- The account-deletion confirmation dialog uses a red (`colorError`) title — the only product-wide pattern where title color (not just an icon or badge) is the signal distinguishing an irreversible action from a routine interruption like session expiry (which uses a neutral title). This color must never be muted or reused for non-destructive confirmations.
- The account-deletion dialog traps focus until dismissed or confirmed, reusing the same focus-trap overlay behavior already used by the session-expired overlay — no interacting with the scrim-covered screen underneath while it's open.
- General overlay conventions apply: a scrim fades in first, the dialog/sheet sits at most one level deep over the base screen, and under reduced-motion settings the scrim/entrance animation is skipped in favor of showing the final state immediately.

## Cross-Story Dependencies

- Story 8.2's narrative text is fetched independently alongside Story 8.1's chart, but visually appears only once the chart from 8.1 is already rendering — 8.1 must ship the chart and its three entry-count states before 8.2's narrative/unavailable states are meaningful to build on top of.
- Story 8.3 depends on the avatar component already built in an earlier epic; it must be reused at a new fixed size, not reimplemented.
- Story 8.5's focus-trap dialog behavior depends on the same focus-trap pattern already implemented for the session-expired overlay elsewhere in the app; reuse it rather than building a second implementation.
- Stories 8.4 and 8.5 both route to the same post-action destination (the login/vault screen) — keep that destination logic shared rather than duplicated between logout and account deletion.
- The whole epic depends on entries existing (for the dashboard to have anything to aggregate) and on the auth session mechanism built in the foundation unit (for logout/deletion to have a session to end).

Relevant epic-8-context.md verbatim (lines as read): - Goal: *"...edit their display name, log out, and permanently delete their account..."* - UX pattern (quoted verbatim): *"Profile name editing: tapping the pencil icon beside the name switches it to an inline editable field and the pencil icon itself changes to a check icon — the only place in the product where an icon's meaning changes rather than just its color. Confirming saves and reverts to display mode; tapping away without confirming also reverts to display mode. There is no separate 'edit profile' screen."* - Technical decision: *"The 52px avatar shown here reuses the same avatar component already built earlier (previously only used at a 40px size) — do not reimplement it."* - Cross-story dependency: *"Story 8.3 depends on the avatar component already built in an earlier epic; it must be reused at a new fixed size, not reimplemented."* ## 5. Prototype UX reference `docs/input/prototype/prototype-extract.md:116`: *"Other elements of Configurações: avatar with editable name/e-mail (pencil becomes a check in edit mode — inline editing); persona cards 'Como a IA responde' (Analítico, Empático, Socrático) **[ext]**; actions 'Sair' and 'Apagar conta' (red)."* Also line 167 confirms `pencil-simple` and `check` are both in the Phosphor icon set already used by the project. Raw markup, `docs/input/prototype/cerne-prototype.html` (Configurações section, decoded from escaped JS template string): ```html
{{ profileInitials }}
{{ profileName }}
{{ profileEmail }}
{{ profileEmail }}
``` JS state/behavior functions (same file): - `toggleEditProfile = () => this.setState(s => ({ editingProfile: !s.editingProfile, nameDraft: s.profileName }))` - `onNameDraftChange = (e) => this.setState({ nameDraft: e.target.value })` - `saveProfile = () => this.setState(s => ({ profileName: s.nameDraft, editingProfile: false }))` - Icon/handler wiring: `editIcon: s.editingProfile ? 'ph-check' : 'ph-pencil-simple'`, `onEditIconClick: s.editingProfile ? this.saveProfile : this.toggleEditProfile` - Initial state: `editingProfile: false, profileName: 'Marina Alves', profileEmail: 'marina.alves@email.com', nameDraft: 'Marina Alves'` - **Note:** the prototype's own JS has no blur/tap-away-to-revert handler wired anywhere (no `onBlur`/outside-tap listener) — epic-8-context.md's "tapping away without confirming also reverts" requirement is a spec addition beyond what the demo actually implements; treat epic-8-context.md as authoritative over the raw prototype behavior here. - Name input's inline style uses `border:1px solid #E1DACB` (1px, unfocused-default weight) — one weight only is shown, no focused/error state demoed for this specific field in the prototype. **Design tokens already available for reuse** (`lib/core/design_tokens.dart`): - `borderWidthDefault = 1` (line 259), `borderWidthEmphasis = 1.5` (line 263) — the two border weights `AppTextField` already uses. - `textFieldContentPadding = EdgeInsets.symmetric(horizontal: spacingMd, vertical: spacingSm)` (lines 546-549). - `avatarSizeSm = 40` / `avatarSizeLg = 52` (lines 253/256), `avatarInitialsPadding` (line 551). - No dedicated "inline edit field" token exists — the plan should reuse `lib/core/widgets/app_text_field.dart`'s `AppTextField` (full file read, 110 lines) rather than hand-rolling a new bordered `TextField`; it already implements default/focused/error border states from these same tokens, `colorSurfaceElevated` fill, and `textFieldContentPadding`. Its `maxLines`/`controller`/`onChanged`/`focusNode` params fit the inline-edit use case directly, though its default chrome (filled background, label/hint) is heavier than the prototype's minimal bordered input — a planner should decide whether to reuse `AppTextField` as-is or build a lighter-weight inline variant. ## 6. Existing similar patterns to reuse - `TextEditingController` usage exists in: `lib/core/widgets/app_text_field.dart`, `lib/features/capture/presentation/cubit/text_entry_cubit.dart`, `lib/features/capture/presentation/widgets/insertion_modal.dart`, `lib/features/chat/presentation/screens/chat_screen.dart`, `lib/features/auth/presentation/screens/auth_screen.dart`. None of these is an "inline tap-to-edit, tap-away-to-revert" pattern specifically — all are persistent form/composer fields. No prior inline-edit affordance exists in `lib/` yet; Story 8.3 is the first. - **`Resource` is explicitly NOT the right shape here.** `lib/core/resource.dart`'s own doc comment (AD-12) says it's for "screens with exactly one data source and one fetch (idle/loading/data/error)... used only where that shape fits... RF02's capture pipeline, RF04's chat stream... each define their own sealed state class instead — never forced into this one." A fire-action-and-watch-saving/error flow is not a fetch lifecycle. - The closest existing precedent for "fire an action, get `Either` back, show saving/error" is **this same file's own `AccountSettingsCubit`/`AccountSettingsState`** (`lib/features/account/presentation/cubit/account_settings_cubit.dart`): a plain (non-sealed, non-Resource) state class with `isSaving: bool` + `errorMessage: String?` fields, a `copyWith`, and a cubit method (`toggleBiometric`) that: emits `isSaving: true` + clears error → awaits the repository call → guards `isClosed` → on `Left` sets `errorMessage` (with a special-cased "superseded" suppression) and `isSaving: false`, on `Right` just clears `isSaving`. This is the pattern to extend (e.g. add `nameErrorMessage`/`isSavingName`/`isEditingName`/`nameDraft` fields to `AccountSettingsState`, and a `startEditingName()`/`updateNameDraft()`/`saveName()`/`cancelEditingName()` set of methods on the same cubit) rather than introducing a second cubit or a `Resource`-shaped one. - `BookmarkState` (`lib/features/chat/domain/entities/bookmark_state.dart`, spec-6-4) is a sealed 4-state (`idle`/`saving`/`saved`/`error(Failure)`) per-item action state, closer to "fire action, track status" than `Resource` — a reasonable alternative shape if the planner prefers a sealed class over flags on `AccountSettingsState`, but note it's scoped to one list item (chat bubble) rather than a singleton screen, so direct reuse would need adaptation. - Export request (spec-7-1) and chat-message retry were checked for a similar shape but no dedicated files named `*retry*`/`*bookmark*` beyond `bookmark_state.dart` and `lib/core/network/retry_interceptor.dart` (an HTTP-layer retry interceptor, unrelated to UI state) exist under `lib/`. ## 7. `account_settings_screen_test.dart` structure `test/features/account/presentation/screens/account_settings_screen_test.dart`: - `_FakeAccountSettingsRepository` (lines 33-80): a plain (non-mocktail) hand-written fake implementing `AccountSettingsRepository` directly — scriptable `setBiometricEnabledResult` (`Either`, defaults to a `Left` failure so tests must opt in to success), a `Completer? setBiometricEnabledGate` to hold calls mid-flight for testing `isSaving`, and a real (non-replay) `StreamController.broadcast()`. **Will need a parallel `displayNameResult`/`nameDraft`-equivalent plus whatever new method Story 8.3 adds to the repository interface.** - `_FakeDashboardRepository` and `_UnusedPendingEntryWriteTracker` (lines 82-146): trivial fakes just to satisfy the widened constructor, unrelated to name editing. - `_buildDashboardCubit`/`_buildNarrativeCubit` (lines 157-177): helper builders, `addTearDown(cubit.close)`. - `_routerWith(Widget screen)` (lines 183-191): wraps the screen in a minimal 2-route `GoRouter` (`/` and `/configuracoes`) because `BackArrowHeader` calls `context.go('/')` and needs a real router ancestor — a bare `MaterialApp` is not enough. - `_pumpScreen(WidgetTester tester)` (lines 208-227): builds a fresh `_FakeAccountSettingsRepository` + `AccountSettingsCubit` pair **inside the test body itself**, not in `setUp()` — explicitly documented reason: `setUp()` runs in a different test-zone than `testWidgets`'s own callback, and a `StreamSubscription` created in the outer zone doesn't reliably get flushed by `tester.pump()`. Any new Story 8.3 test must follow this same "construct cubit inside the `testWidgets` body" convention, not in `setUp()`. - Pumps via `MaterialApp.router(routerConfig: router)`. ## 8. DI registration and routing `lib/features/account/account_injection.dart` (38 lines) — `registerAccountFeature()`, called from `setupCoreDependencies()` right after `registerVaultFeature()`: - `sl.registerLazySingleton(() => AccountRemoteDataSource(sl()))` - `sl.registerLazySingleton(() => AccountSettingsRepositoryImpl(remoteDataSource: sl()), dispose: (repository) => repository.dispose())` - `sl.registerLazySingleton(() => AccountSettingsCubit(sl()), dispose: (cubit) => cubit.close())` No new registrations exist yet for name editing — if Story 8.3 adds a new use case/second data method on the existing repository (recommended, since it's the same `account-settings-update` function), no new DI entries are needed beyond whatever constructor params change on `AccountSettingsCubit`/`AccountSettingsRepositoryImpl`. Routing: `lib/core/navigation/app_router.dart:137-144` — `GoRoute(path: AppRoutePaths.configuracoes, builder: (context, state) => AccountSettingsScreen(cubit: sl(), dashboardCubit: sl(), narrativeCubit: sl()))`. `AccountSettingsRepository` is also injected directly into `buildAppRouter(...)` itself (line 68) and read synchronously at `VaultLockScreen`'s route builder (line 91) for `currentBiometricEnabled` — any new repository field/stream Story 8.3 adds must not break this synchronous read pattern or the constructor signature of `buildAppRouter`. ## Key open design question for the planner Since `docs/input/requirements.md` has no FR text or acceptance criteria for name editing (§4), and the backend's `users` data-model table in that same doc omits `display_name` even though the frozen OpenAPI schema has it, the authoritative UX contract is **epic-8-context.md's own prose** (quoted in full above), not a numbered FR. The planner should cite epic-8-context.md directly as the acceptance-criteria source for Story 8.3, the same way spec-8-1/8-2 already did (both existing spec files reference epic-8-context.md's "Requirements & Constraints"/"UX & Interaction Patterns" sections, confirmed by their presence as siblings `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-8-1-*.md` / `spec-8-2-*.md`).
